Let's get something straight out of the way at the very beginning: free speech does exist on Reddit. Not pure free speech (as you will still get censored if you dox someone or post illegal material), but for the most part, it does exist, as de-facto free speech. I can write a very critical post/comment on reddit, I can call the reddit admins shitheads if I'd like and not have it be removed. You can, for the most part, say whatever you want, the same way you can say whatever you want in a public space. I can only cite one instance in which an admin intervened and actually censored something, and that was during the Sears ordeal years back.

The caveat here is that Reddit lets the mods decide what their rules for their subs are. That means there are restrictions on speech at a local level (at the subreddit level). This does not mean that free speech doesn't exist on the site itself, as one could simply post the offending content on another sub where such rules don't exist. Most of these mod instated restrictions are reasonable and have more to do with quality control, e.g., you can't post editorials to news subs, etc.

Often you'll have people who break those rules and then cry censorship, particularly if it is a major sub. My contention is that this is not censorship, it's just a mod/sub - user mismatch.

Take for example a situation where someone wants to post an article on the dangers of vaccines (a conspiratorial type of topic) on a major, default sub on medicine. Needless to say, if the sub wishes to hold itself to a high standard of quality, they will remove it. They don't need conspiracy nuts posting conspiracy stuff on a sub like that. The offending poster will understandably view that as censorship. That is the nature of the problem. It's not that reddit itself or any of the admins actively went out of their way to censor them, it's just that there was no space available for them to post what they want in a satisfactory manner.

This is one of the things that Voat failed to understand. They saw a bunch of users complaining about censorship, and took it the wrong way. They made the mistake of embracing free speech as an identity and made it their mission.

There is no benefit to this. They could've not said anything and had de-facto free speech instead of making free speech their identity. I mean, think about this. Imagine being a normal, average user. Say you want to discuss the latest cars. You're not thinking, "Am I going to be censored?" You just won't care. It's a non-issue. Who will care? The hate speech people, the extremists and radicals. That's what making free speech your motto does, it attracts the worst of the worst. Most people reading this aren't concerned with "hmm, if I post something hateful, I might get deleted" because more likely than not, they aren't posting something that will raise that question. Simply put, free speech isn't a selling point to an ordinary user because free speech and censorship isn't a concern to them.

By making free speech their mission, they've offered normal, average, typical users nothing of benefit. On the other hand, it greatly benefits the racists, sexist, homophobes and other hate oriented users by providing an open venue for them. The malcontents of reddit flocked there instead, not the best creators of content. This is why if you look at voat, a large percentage of it is extremely controversial stuff involving race or something like that that the most of us generally do not give a shit about or wish to discuss.

It's also created a culture of "anything goes" that has led to poor quality control. Take a look at /v/news for an example of this. Blatantly misleading titles and the sources are complete shit. There is no quality control because now if something gets deleted, it's censorship. It's created a reluctance on the part of the mods to do their job because they don't want to go against the free speech culture. Moreover, it's created some serious problems for Voat because it's inundated with racists and other undesireable types now. This isn't good for Voat, unless it wants to become a 4chan type of community. It also limits Voat because it would've been great to have the flexibility to do a little "management" during an early stage of growth like this, e.g., a little short term pruning here or there to make the site look good and attractive to the greater public. Nothing too heavy handed or extreme. The world isn't going to condemn you because you deleted something that advocated genocide. Instead, you've got a situation where the first page of /v/all is often cluttered with unappealing garbage and any administrative action you take will be scrutinized through the lens of whether speech was restricted.

It's going to just look bad if Voat backs down in some form or another from it's free speech stance now, because they will inevitably run into some situations where they are forced to remove some stuff due to pragmatic and practical reasons.

As an aside: there are people who are anti-SJW claiming that they are being censored by SJWs. That has nothing to do with free speech. Think of the internet as a public space like the streets, if you say something racist out the open, chances are you are going to get shouted down. This is the same thing. The only place where they will be safe is where the place is a complete shithole filled with like-minded people.

TLDR: De-facto, unspoken free speech is what you want, not "we're about free speech, everyone come over and post all the hateful stuff you want!"
